discovery: Optical lattice clocks and precision measurement at the 10^-18 level

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms in a 'magic wavelength' lattice so that the trap light leaves the clock transition unperturbed. This lets many atoms be interrogated at once without motional or light-shift penalties. Ye turned the concept into the most precise measuring instruments ever built. With ultrastable lasers, frequency-comb metrology and control of quantum many-body effects, his clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and resolved the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample. Katori's transportable clocks measured height differences through general relativity at the Tokyo Skytree. These clocks now lead the way to redefining the SI second, and they are sensitive probes of variations in fundamental constants, dark matter and relativistic geodesy. This is careful atomic physics that opens fundamental questions to laboratory test, in the tradition of Ramsey, Hall and Hänsch.
